findings.summary: Page 2 is titled "HTTP/3 and QPACK (cont.)" but more than half of it teaches the next chapter, "When Each Version Helps", so a learner meets the version-comparison material under the QPACK heading.
findings.evidence: Page 2 runs from QPACK material ("Base and relative indexing make references position-independent", "Finding HTTP/3 At All") straight into "What Is Actually Optimized" — "HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 optimize latency and connection efficiency, not raw throughput" — followed by the two verdict tables, "The CPU Footnote", "Beyond Browsers", and the full `Property / 1.1 / 2 / 3` comparison table, all of which are chapter-9 points.
findings.fix: End page 2 after the `Alt-Svc`/SVCB/fallback block (the last HTTP/3-discovery point), and start a new page titled "When Each Version Helps (and When It Doesn't)" at the "What Is Actually Optimized" heading, carrying the verdict tables, CPU footnote, "Beyond Browsers", and comparison table with it.

findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a part label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of HTTP/2 & HTTP/3 HANDBOOK. Your page is slow because of round trips, not bandwidth — and every HTTP/1.1 trick you learned (sharding, spriting, base64 inlining) now actively fights HTTP/2."
findings.fix: Open with the hook and demote the part label: "Your page is slow because of round trips, not bandwidth — and every HTTP/1.1 trick you learned (sharding, spriting, base64 inlining) now actively fights HTTP/2. Part 2 of HTTP/2 & HTTP/3 HANDBOOK: 10 pages of study notes on ..."

findings.summary: The comparison table credits HTTP/2 with saving a handshake round trip over HTTP/1.1, which it does not — both run the identical TCP+TLS handshake, so the ~3 vs ~2 split silently compares TLS 1.2 against TLS 1.3.
findings.fix: Hold TLS version constant: make the row "handshake RTT (TLS 1.3)" with values "2", "2", "1 (0-RTT: 0)", and if the TLS 1.2 case matters add a separate note that HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 are both ~3 RTT over TLS 1.2 — the saving comes from TLS 1.3, not from h2.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: Page 3 carries the title "When Each Version Helps (and When It Doesn't)" but its bulk is the Debugging/Gotchas chapter, while the three genuine chapter-9 items it does hold are orphaned fragments of a discussion already completed on page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 3 opens with "Adoption Is An Edge Toggle", the "Which version should I benchmark with?" Q&A and "Where 0-RTT Pays" ("High-RTT paths make the saved handshake round trip real user-visible time") — commentary on tables the learner last saw a page earlier — then switches to "Seven Ways To Waste h2" and "Tools That Show The Truth" with `curl --http2 -v`, `nghttp -nv`, which are chapter-10 gotchas and debug tools; page 4's opening `Tool / Shows` table then continues that same tool list under the correct title.
findings.fix: Move "Adoption Is An Edge Toggle", the benchmark Q&A and "Where 0-RTT Pays" up so they sit immediately after the HTTP/3 verdict table and comparison table on the "When Each Version Helps" page, and move "Seven Ways To Waste h2" and the curl/nghttp code block onto the "Debugging, Gotchas, and Recap" page directly above its `Tool / Shows` table.

findings.summary: The fallback diagram teaches a serial timeout chain and the paragraph immediately under it denies that clients behave serially, leaving the learner with two incompatible models of the same mechanism.
findings.evidence: Diagram nodes: "h3 attempt", "timeout", "h2 over TCP", "h1.1" — followed by "Clients race the options rather than failing over serially, so users experience slower loads, not error pages."
findings.fix: Redraw the diagram as a race (parallel "h3 attempt" and "h2 over TCP" branches converging on "first to complete wins", with "h1.1" as the last-resort branch), or change the paragraph to state that the timeout chain is the fallback order while racing is what hides it from the user.

findings.summary: HTTP/3 unidirectional stream types are variable-length integers, not a single type byte.
findings.evidence: "Unidirectional streams carry control data, tagged by a type byte"
findings.fix: Reword to "tagged by a leading stream-type varint" — the four defined types (control 0x00, push 0x01, QPACK encoder 0x02, decoder 0x03) happen to be one byte, but reserved/greased types are longer.

findings.summary: The section titled "Seven Ways To Waste h2" lists eight items.
findings.evidence: "heading","text":"Seven Ways To Waste h2" followed by two bullet blocks of four items each (sharding/spriting, HOL assumption, CDN-to-origin h1.1, uppercase headers, `Connection: keep-alive`, `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE`, 0-RTT replay, new-port myth)
findings.fix: Retitle to "Eight Ways To Waste h2", or drop one bullet (the two h3-specific ones — 0-RTT replay and the 443/UDP myth — are the odd ones out under an h2 heading).

findings.summary: The answer marker under the question heading renders at a near-zero font size and is illegible.
findings.evidence: A roughly 6px-tall glyph reading "Ans→" sits at the left margin directly beneath "Which version should I benchmark with?", while the answer bullets beside it are set at normal body size.
findings.fix: Set the Q&A answer-marker element to the same body font size as the bullets it labels (or drop the marker) so it renders legibly.

findings.summary: "high-BDP paths" uses an abbreviation the handbook never expands or defines anywhere in the syllabus or content.
findings.evidence: "Leaving `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` at 64 KB on high-BDP paths, then blaming the network"
findings.fix: Write it as "high bandwidth-delay-product (BDP) paths — high bandwidth × high RTT", or replace with the concrete case already taught in the flow-control chapter: "64 KB over a 100 ms RTT caps a stream near 5 Mbps".

findings.summary: The heading "Seven Ways To Waste h2" labels a list of eight items, three of which are HTTP/3 or 0-RTT mistakes rather than h2 mistakes.
findings.evidence: Heading "Seven Ways To Waste h2" over two bullet blocks of four items each, including "Treating 0-RTT as free when it is replayable" and "Believing HTTP/3 needs a new port; it is 443/UDP".
findings.fix: Retitle to "Eight Ways To Waste Your Upgrade" (or split into "Five Ways To Waste h2" and a separate short "Three Ways To Waste h3" group) so the count and the version scope both match the bullets.

findings.summary: The tooling table implies Wireshark's SSLKEYLOGFILE decryption is TCP-only and that QUIC/HTTP-3 headers stay opaque on capture, but Wireshark has decrypted QUIC and dissected HTTP/3 (including headers) since 3.6.
findings.fix: Change the Wireshark row's "Shows" cell to "decrypted TLS over TCP *and* QUIC/h3 (3.6+)" and change the qlog row to something like "endpoint-side QUIC event log: congestion, streams, RTT" — qlog's value is transport internals a capture can't show, not header visibility.

findings.summary: The degradation diagram shows serial failover with a timeout, directly contradicting the paragraph beneath it and the Happy-Eyeballs racing claim on page 2.
findings.evidence: diagram nodes ["h3 attempt","timeout","h2 over TCP","h1.1"] followed by "Clients race the options rather than failing over serially"
findings.fix: Replace the diagram's linear chain with a race depiction — e.g. nodes "h3 (UDP) + h2 (TCP) raced in parallel" → "first to complete wins" → "h1.1 if no ALPN upgrade" — so it matches both the paragraph and the page-2 sidebox.
